title: Are You Humiliating Students Without Even Knowing it? knowing-it/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin examines the harm caused by reflexive dismissive reactions ('Why on earth would you want to do that?') to students' unusual questions or ideas, arguing these off-the-cuff comments can be deeply humiliating even though they feel harmless to the adult in the moment. He illustrates the point with a personal anecdote: receiving a dismissive, unsigned email criticizing one of his articles, and describing how the sting of that experience—despite his professional thick skin—helped him understand the outsized emotional impact such reactions have on impressionable students. Linsin argues that teachers forget students carry a wide range of perspectives and sensitivities, and that dismissing a student's earnestly offered idea can make them feel foolish and demoralized, gradually eroding their willingness to share and their sense of possibility. His recommendation is not that teachers must always agree, but that they must take students' ideas and questions seriously and protect their dignity when responding.
points: Reflexive dismissive reactions to unusual student questions or ideas (e.g., "Why on earth would you want to do that?") can feel harmless to adults but are deeply humiliating to students.
Linsin illustrates the emotional impact through a personal anecdote about receiving a dismissive, unsigned reader email criticizing one of his articles.
Teachers often forget that students carry a wide range of personal perspectives and sensitivities shaped by their own experiences.
Dismissing a student's earnestly offered idea can make them feel demoralized and gradually erode their willingness to share and their sense of possibility.
The recommendation is not unconditional agreement, but taking students' ideas and questions seriously and protecting their dignity in every response.
quotes: They are comments that roll off the tongue without second thought.
You see, what we may innocently describe as a way to shake a quixotic student into reality is actually one of the most hurtful and humiliating things you can ever do to them.
We forget that our students represent a kaleidoscope of different perspectives and sensibilities.
The humiliation of having an idea dismissed out of hand was brought home for me in a small way this past week. You see, I was on the other end of someone’s incredulity, and it hurt. It really did.
And the more heart and soul and thought that goes into an idea, the more destructive such reactions can be. It makes the person on the receiving end feel . . . well, stupid.
When you don’t take their ideas, questions, and curiosities seriously, you don’t take them seriously. And every time you dismiss their thinking as foolish, they grow a bit more jaded and demoralized.
